PostgreSQL GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes are designed for data values that contain multiple component values, such as arrays or documents [S1, S2]. They are intended for cases where the items to be indexed are composite values, and queries need to search for specific element values (keys) that appear within those composite items [S2, S3].

An inverted index is organized by storing a separate entry for each component value (key) rather than for the item as a whole [S1, S2]. Specifically, a GIN index stores a set of (key, posting list) pairs, where a posting list is a set of row IDs (heap pointers) in which the key occurs [S2, S4]. The same row ID can appear in multiple posting lists, since an item can contain more than one key, but each key value is stored only once, making the index very compact for repeated keys [S2].

Internally, a GIN index contains a B-tree index constructed over the keys [S4]. Each tuple in a leaf page of this B-tree contains either a pointer to a B-tree of heap pointers (called a "posting tree") or a simple list of heap pointers (a "posting list") if the list is small enough to fit into a single index tuple along with the key value [S4].

PostgreSQL's Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC) gives each SQL statement a consistent view by allowing it to see a snapshot of the data (a database version) as it existed at some point in time, regardless of the current state of the underlying data [S1]. For example, in the default Read Committed isolation level, a SELECT query sees a snapshot of the database as of the instant the query begins, viewing only data committed before the query started [S4]. This prevents statements from viewing inconsistent data produced by concurrent transactions performing updates on the same data rows [S1].

MVCC reduces read-write contention by eschewing the traditional locking methodologies used by other database systems [S1]. Under MVCC, locks acquired for reading data do not conflict with locks acquired for writing data [S1]. As a result, reading never blocks writing, and writing never blocks reading, which minimizes lock contention and allows for reasonable performance in multiuser environments [S1].
